tagline: Don’t stop the bloom. Give it another path.

problem.question: How might we advance the sustainable management of seasonal jellyfish blooms in coastal environments?
problem.context: Early warning already exists. The challenge starts after it: manage large, continuous swarms with less manual effort, less specialised equipment and less field support, with no harm to marine life and no redesign of plant systems.

solution: Two full-depth nets stand across the intake channel at 20°, ahead of every intake. Water passes through. Jellyfish are held back, so the plant’s own flow sweeps them along the nets into one funnel. A bucket elevator lifts them in water over the breakwater, and gravity carries them 2 km down the coast. No boats chasing the bloom: crews only swap panels. Plant systems unchanged.
technical: 2 million m³/h through a 140 × 12 m channel runs at 0.33 m/s. A 20° net splits that: 0.11 m/s through the mesh, inside the 0.12 m/s limit used for fish screens, and 0.31 m/s along it, so animals should slide, not pin. Any channel needs at least flow ÷ (depth × 0.12 m/s) of net. At 0.12 m of head the float line dips: cooling comes first.
features: Fish-screen speed. 50 cm bars keep turtles out. Bycatch untested.
Nets reach from surface to seabed.
A second net 60 m behind catches them.
The float line dips. Cooling comes first.
Nets need none. Model: 96 t held for 5 h.
Sonar warns 30 min ahead in the model. It needs no light.
Load cells flag swaps, about every 4 weeks. Out off-season.
No pump at all: a bucket elevator lifts them in water. Survival test planned.
80 mm net A, then 30 mm net B for small and soft bells.
